hook.text: A lung on a chip the size of a USB stick — microfluidic devices recreate organ function with living human cells.

buildup.text: Channels lined with human cells mimic blood flow and tissue interfaces — mechanical stretching simulates breathing in a lung chip.

discovery.text: Wyss Institute's lung-on-a-chip replicated pulmonary edema from drug toxicity — something cell cultures and animal models missed.

twist.text: Connecting multiple organ chips creates a body-on-a-chip — drug metabolism in the liver chip affects toxicity in the heart chip.

climax.text: The FDA now accepts organ-on-chip data to support drug applications — a step toward replacing animal testing.

punchline.text: Shrink a body to a chip — organs-on-chips test drugs on human biology without risk.

quiz.question: What does a body-on-a-chip achieve by connecting multiple organ chips?
options: It creates a full-sized artificial organ for transplantation
It models how drug metabolism in one organ affects toxicity in others, mimicking whole-body pharmacology
It grows a complete human immune system on a single chip

details.summary: Organs-on-chips are microfluidic devices containing human cells arranged in organ-like architecture with fluid flow, mechanical forces, and tissue-tissue interfaces that mimic real organ function. They provide more accurate drug testing than animal models or static cell cultures.
details.whyItMatters: Drug failures in clinical trials cost billions and result from poor prediction by animal models. Organs-on-chips with human cells can predict human drug responses more accurately, potentially reducing drug development failures and replacing animal
takeaways: Microfluidic channels mimic blood flow and mechanical forces of real organs
Human cells in organ-like architecture predict drug responses better than animals
Multi-organ chips model drug metabolism and interactions across organ systems

faq.question: How does a lung-on-a-chip work?
faq.answer: A flexible membrane separates two channels. Human lung epithelial cells grow on one side exposed to air, while endothelial cells line the other side with flowing nutrient media mimicking blood. Cyclic vacuum stretching mimics breathing movements.

faq.question: Could organs-on-chips eliminate animal testing?
faq.answer: The FDA Modernization Act 2.0 no longer mandates animal testing for drug approval, and organ-on-chip data is increasingly accepted. Full replacement will take years as validation data accumulates, but the trajectory is toward significant reduction in animal use for drug development.
